segments.say: If the situation shapes whether we help, then it should be possible to prepare people for the situations. That is the practical promise of this whole field. And psychologists have tested it, beginning with a simple idea: teach people about the bystander effect and see if they behave differently.

In the late 1970s, a team of psychologists designed a short study. Some students attended a lecture about the bystander effect, including the research on diffusion of responsibility. Others heard a lecture on a different topic. Some time later, the students were placed in a staged emergency, to see whether the lecture had made a difference.

The students did not know that the later scene was connected to the lecture. They were walking past a person who had apparently collapsed. Those who had heard the lecture about bystander behaviour were more likely to stop and help than those who had heard the other lecture. A short piece of teaching about the pitfalls of crowds appeared to make students more helpful.

show.what: Increasing helping rates through information dissemination: teaching pays

segments.say: The study was small and has not been repeated many times, so it is best treated as encouraging rather than conclusive. But it matches a wider finding: that knowing about a trap can help people avoid it.

show.title: What the lecture might have changed
items: Awareness that crowds can freeze people
A habit of questioning the calm of others

segments.say: Since then, many programmes have been developed to teach bystander skills, especially to young adults, mostly with the aim of reducing sexual violence and bullying. These programmes typically teach people to notice risky situations, to take responsibility, and to practise safe ways of intervening.

Victoria Banyard and her colleagues at the University of New Hampshire developed a community-based approach in which every person is seen as a potential bystander and helper, and not as a potential perpetrator or victim. They tested a training programme with college students, comparing them with a group who did not receive it, and reported improvements in attitudes and in reported willingness to act.

show.what: Sexual violence prevention through bystander education: an experimental evaluation

segments.say: Reviews of these programmes find that they tend to increase people's intentions and reports of intervening, though effects on actual harmful behaviour are less clear. Researchers continue to refine them, and are cautious about claims. The consistent finding is that practical, skills-based training works better than lectures alone.

The range of options matters. Not everyone is comfortable confronting a stranger, and nobody should put themselves in danger. Good programmes teach several ways of helping, from distracting the person at risk to getting help from someone else.

show.title: What good bystander training includes
items: A range of safe options, not only direct confrontation

segments.say: Researchers and educators often describe a few basic choices for a bystander. You can intervene directly, if it's safe. You can distract, by creating an interruption. You can delegate, by getting someone else to help, such as security or a staff member. And you can delay, by checking in with the person afterwards.

These are practical rather than scientific categories, and they appear in many training programmes. What the research supports is the broader principle behind them: that having a plan, and knowing there's more than one way to act, makes people more likely to do something.

show.title: Four ways to help
items: Direct: speak up if it is safe
Delegate: ask someone in authority to help

segments.say: This is liberating. Helping does not have to mean a dramatic confrontation. Quietly asking a person if they're all right, sitting beside someone who looks uncomfortable, or telling a bartender about a worrying situation are all forms of help. They're modest, and they work.

show.sub: You don't need to be a hero

segments.say: There's good evidence that rehearsing a response makes it easier to carry out when the time comes. Psychologists call such a plan an implementation intention, an if-then rule that links a situation to an action.

Peter Gollwitzer and Paschal Sheeran combined results from ninety-four studies and found that people who formed an if-then plan, such as, if I see X, then I will do Y, were substantially more likely to follow through on their goals than people who only formed the intention. The effect was of medium to large size.

show.what: Implementation intentions and goal achievement: a meta-analysis of effects and processes

segments.say: A plan like this removes a decision from the moment of stress. You don't have to decide whether to act. You've already decided, and only have to carry it out.

show.title: If-then plans for helping
items: If someone looks distressed, then I will ask if they are okay
If I see a crowd standing still, then I will check what is wrong
If someone is being harassed, then I will stand near them and ask a question
If I can't act safely, then I will get help

segments.say: Four terms from this chapter. Bystander training teaches people to recognise and respond to situations. An implementation intention is an if-then plan. To delegate is to ask someone better placed to act. And skills-based training means practising actions, not only learning facts.

show.title: Words to keep from this chapter

segments.say: Here is how to make your own plan. Choose one situation where you tend to hesitate, such as seeing someone upset in public. Write an if-then sentence for it. Say it aloud twice. And review it in a week. Picture this scene: a woman who always freezes when a stranger seems unwell has a plan. If someone looks faint, I will ask, are you all right? On a crowded train, a man leans against the door looking grey. She asks. He says he needs to sit. Three people make room. The plan took ten seconds to write, and it changed the minute.

show.title: Make your own if-then plan
items: Choose one situation where you hesitate

segments.say: A pause to think about preparation. What would you like to be able to do if something happened in front of you? Many people say they would like to know first aid, to stay calm, or to know what to say. Those are all things that can be learned. If you've never done a first aid course, think about whether this might be the time. And think about the plan we wrote. If someone looks distressed, then I will ask if they are all right. If I see a crowd standing still, then I will check what is wrong. Sentences like these seem too simple to matter, but the studies suggest that they work, precisely because they spare us from deciding in the moment. Who could you practise with? A friend, a family member or a colleague might enjoy saying them aloud together. Preparation is a quiet form of courage.

show.title: Pause and reflect
items: What would I like to be able to do in an emergency?
Have I ever learned first aid?
Which if-then plan could I write?

segments.say: An empty classroom, set up for practice. Skills are built in rooms like this, where people can try, stumble and try again, long before the moment that counts. The most encouraging finding in this chapter is also the simplest: people who were taught about the pitfalls of crowds did better. Knowledge of the trap is part of the way out of it, and you now have that knowledge.

If you have ever wished you had known what to do, you are in good company. The research is encouraging: a little knowledge and a little rehearsal go a long way. You can prepare to be kind, and that preparation is itself an act of kindness.

So what did we learn? That teaching about the bystander effect made students more helpful in one study. That skills-based programmes seem to improve intentions and reported action. That there are several safe ways to help. And that if-then plans make action more likely.
In the next chapter, we'll move from pavements to screens, and ask what happens to helping when the crowd is invisible.
